title: The Limp Across the Empires: Zamość to the Landwehr Canal
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Zamość, the house on Ulica Staszica
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: In a timber merchant's house in a walled Renaissance town of the Lublin Governorate, Eliasz Luxemburg and Lina Loewenstein have their fifth and last child, a daughter registered as Rozalia. The empire that keeps the register is Russian; the town is Polish; the household is Jewish, commercial, and bookish, and German, Polish and Hebrew cross the same table. Nothing in the room is revolutionary. The house is number 37 on Ulica Staszica, and it is the town's own record of the address, not a civil register, that identifies it.
suggested_refs: The birth house at ul. Staszica 37, Zamość, identified by the town's own record of the address

stops.name: Warsaw, the move and the hip
stops.date_confidence: Move to Warsaw attested to 1873; no month recorded. The childhood illness is dated only approximately, to around her fifth year, and the diagnosis is genuinely unsettled: biographies give congenital dislocation of the hip or a misdiagnosed tubercular disease, and no clinical record survives to decide between them.
stops.campa: The family leaves Zamość for the capital when she is two, for the trade and for the schools. Somewhere near her fifth year an ailment of the hip takes hold and she is kept in bed for the better part of a year. What it was is not recoverable; what it left is. She walks the rest of her life with one leg shorter than the other, a gait every police description and every hostile cartoonist will use, and she is a small woman in a movement of large men who shout. She reads constantly through the year in bed.
suggested_refs: The Nettl and Froelich biographies, which carry the two competing diagnoses side by side
sources: biographical tradition (Nettl, Froelich), no surviving clinical record

stops.name: Warsaw, the Second Girls' Gymnasium
stops.date_confidence: The leaving certificate is dated 14 June 1887 and survives in the German Federal Archives (Nachlass Rosa Luxemburg, NY 4002). Attendance from 1884 per de.wikipedia. The recurring story that a gold medal was withheld from her for oppositional conduct is repeated across the biographies with no administrative document behind it.
stops.campa: The school is Russian-administered and holds Jewish admissions to a quota, and she is inside the quota. She finishes at the top and takes her certificate on the fourteenth of June, at sixteen, having already joined a conspiracy. The story that runs through every biography, that the gold medal was withheld because her bearing toward authority was oppositional, has no paper behind it. What has paper is the certificate itself, folded away, carried out of the Russian Empire, kept for half a century by people who moved often, and catalogued at last in Berlin under the shelfmark NY 4002.
suggested_refs: The 1887 school certificate in the Nachlass Rosa Luxemburg, Bundesarchiv
sources: German Federal Archives, weimar.bundesarchiv.de, Nachlass Rosa Luxemburg

stops.name: Warsaw, the Second Proletariat
stops.date_confidence: Year attested, month not recorded. The date is placed at the head of 1887 to order the segment.
stops.campa: The first Proletariat party was broken in 1886, its leaders hanged at the Citadel, and what is left of it in Warsaw meets in rooms without a name on the door. She joins the cell that calls itself the Second Proletariat while she is still a schoolgirl, and she will not belong to a wholly legal movement again, in any country she lives in. The discipline is that of a clandestine organization: false names, couriers, a press moved before the police can find it. In Russian Poland at this date the whole of political life is a criminal offense.
suggested_refs: The remnant Proletariat cells of Warsaw, 1886-1889

stops.name: The Prussian frontier, out of the empire
stops.date_confidence: Flight from Russian Poland and arrival in Zurich in early 1889 are attested; no month or day. The crossing point is nowhere named in the sources and this coordinate is an explicit placeholder on a common Congress Poland to Prussia rail frontier. The often repeated detail that she was smuggled out under straw in a peasant's cart rests on later recollection, with no police or border record behind it.
stops.campa: Arrest is close enough that the comrades move her out. She crosses the frontier of the Russian Empire without papers and does not see Warsaw again for sixteen years. The scene the biographies love, a girl hidden under straw in a cart while a priest talks the guards past her, comes from recollection rather than from any record, and the record does not name the road, the village or the day. What the record has is the other end of the journey: by the early months of 1889 she is in Zurich.
suggested_refs: The escape-under-straw tradition, common to Nettl and Froelich, unsupported by border or police documents

segments.name: Zurich: The Doctorate and the Polish Question

stops.name: Zurich, matriculation at the university
stops.date_confidence: October 1889 per de.wikipedia; en.wikipedia gives 1890, which is the weaker reading against arrival in early 1889. Day not recorded. The move from the philosophy faculty to law and state sciences is dated 1892 by pl.wikipedia.
stops.campa: Zurich takes women on terms almost no other European university will, and it fills accordingly with students out of the Russian Empire who cannot study at home. She enrolls in natural science and mathematics, botany among them, then in 1892 moves across to law, public administration and political economy. The city is a small crowded republic of exiles arguing in four languages about a revolution none of them can reach, and within four years she is contesting credentials there with men twice her age. She is eighteen when she matriculates, and she walks with a limp.
suggested_refs: The old main building of the University of Zurich on the Raemistrasse

stops.name: Zurich, Leo Jogiches
stops.date_confidence: The relationship is dated to the early Zurich years and ran roughly fifteen years; no precise beginning is recorded. The date orders the segment. General Zurich coordinates; no meeting address is documented.
stops.campa: Leo Jogiches arrives out of Vilna with money, an organizer's temperament and an absolute refusal to sign his own name to anything. What begins between them lasts some fifteen years and is never separable into private and political halves: he builds the apparatus, she writes, they quarrel over both in the same letters. He keeps himself out of print so completely that his role has to be reconstructed from her correspondence. They will be arrested together in Warsaw, and he will outlive her by eight weeks.
suggested_refs: The Luxemburg-Jogiches correspondence, principal source for his otherwise unsigned organizational work

stops.name: Zurich, the congress and the credentials
stops.date_confidence: Congress dated 6-12 August 1893 by de.wikipedia; the stop is placed on its opening day.
stops.campa: At the Zurich congress of the Second International she comes forward to be seated as a Polish delegate and the Polish Socialist Party moves to keep her out. The quarrel is not procedural. The PPS holds that Poland must first be independent; she holds that Russian Poland's industry is already bound into the Russian market, that its workers and Russian workers face the same state, and that a national program will divide them. She does not abandon the position afterward, and it costs her Polish readers for a century. She is twenty-two. She loses the vote.
suggested_refs: Proceedings of the Zurich congress of the Second International, August 1893

stops.name: Paris, Sprawa Robotnicza and the SDKP
stops.date_confidence: Year attested, no month. The place is in conflict between the sources: the chronology has the paper and the party founded among the Zurich exiles, the geographical record places the founding of Sprawa Robotnicza in Paris. The conflict is left standing. The coordinate is a Left Bank emigre-quarter placeholder, not a documented address.
stops.campa: With Jogiches, Julian Marchlewski and Adolf Warski she founds a paper, Sprawa Robotnicza, the Workers' Cause, and around it the Social Democracy of the Kingdom of Poland. It is a party of exiles publishing for readers who can be jailed for holding the paper, smuggled east in the linings of coats. Its founding argument is her argument at the congress that year: class before nation, across the frontiers of three partitioning empires. Where the founding actually took place, Zurich or Paris, the sources do not agree.
suggested_refs: Sprawa Robotnicza, organ of the SDKP, from 1893

stops.name: London, the congress resolution on self-determination
stops.date_confidence: Congress July 1896; day not fixed here. The credentials fight with the PPS belongs to Zurich 1893, not to London: en.wikipedia records the London congress as passing a compromise resolution on the right of all nations to self-determination without specific mention of Poland. Coordinate is a central London placeholder; the venue was not confirmed.
stops.campa: The International meets in London and settles the national question the way large bodies settle questions they cannot decide: it affirms the right of all nations to self-determination and declines to name Poland. Both sides read the resolution as a victory and both sides go on printing what they printed before. She takes the omission as the substance, and goes back to arguing tariffs and freight, which is the ground she has chosen. Whether the silence about Poland was a concession to her case or an evasion of it, the text of the resolution does not say, and the congress record reached here does not settle it either.
suggested_refs: The 1896 London congress resolution on national self-determination

stops.name: Zurich, Die industrielle Entwicklung Polens
stops.date_confidence: Promoted magna cum laude in May 1897 per de.wikipedia; day not recorded.
stops.campa: The dissertation is not a polemic and that is its weapon. She works through tariffs, rail freight, textile output and the Russian market for Lodz cloth, and shows that Russian Poland's capitalism has grown into the empire's economy rather than beside it. What she lost on a show of hands at the congress four years earlier she proves here in numbers. She is twenty-six, promoted magna cum laude, a doctor of law of the University of Zurich and one of very few women in Europe holding the degree. Its English translator will call it the first comprehensive economic history of Poland ever published.
suggested_refs: Die industrielle Entwicklung Polens (Leipzig, 1898), and the translator's historical note to the English edition
sources: marxists.org, translator's historical note to 'The Industrial Development of Poland'

stops.name: Basel, the marriage of convenience
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: She marries Gustav Luebeck, the son of a friend, in order to become a German subject. There is no household and no pretense of one. The marriage is a document, procured because a Russian subject cannot speak, publish or stand for office inside Germany, and Germany holds the largest workers' party in the world. Within a month of the ceremony she is in Berlin and inside that party. Of everything she does in these years it is the coldest and the most practical. They divorce in 1903.
suggested_refs: The Basel marriage record of 19 April 1898

stops.name: Berlin, Cuxhavener Strasse 2
stops.date_confidence: Date and address attested by de.wikipedia. Coordinate corrected to the street's actual position in the Hansaviertel.
stops.campa: She arrives in Berlin on the twelfth of May with a German passport, a doctorate, no reputation in Germany and no money. The SPD has a million voters, a press, a bureaucracy, deputies in the Reichstag and a theory that history will hand it power. She joins it, and inside a year she is in its central arguments; twenty years on it will expel her. For now there is a rented room in the Hansaviertel, on the Cuxhavener Strasse, and a capital she has never lived in and cannot yet write for.
suggested_refs: Cuxhavener Strasse 2, Berlin-Hansaviertel, her first German address

stops.name: Upper Silesia, the Polish-speaking districts
stops.date_confidence: The 1898 Reichstag campaign is attested; the month is not, and no individual speaking site is documented. The coordinate marks Oppeln as representative of the Upper Silesian districts she worked.
stops.campa: The party has an immediate use for a new member who speaks Polish: the mining and steel districts of Upper Silesia vote in German elections and pray, argue and strike in Polish, and the SPD has been losing them to the Catholic Centre. She is sent out to speak, and it is the first German work she is given. The argument she carries into the coalfield is the one she made in Zurich, that Polish workers under a German state and Polish workers under a Russian one are in the same fight and not in a national one. Not one of the halls she spoke in is named in the record.
suggested_refs: The 1898 Reichstag election in the Upper Silesian constituencies

stops.name: Dresden, the Saechsische Arbeiterzeitung
stops.date_confidence: Editorship attested to 1898-1899; the starting month is not recorded and September is used to order the segment.
stops.campa: Six months in Germany and she is made chief editor of a party daily. It goes badly and quickly. She writes as she argues, straight at the target and without the emollient the paper's staff are used to, and the older men on the board will not be edited by a twenty-seven-year-old out of Zamosc. She leaves without the editorship and with her name known in every party office in Saxony. The tenure is measured in months, and the sources do not record which month it began.
suggested_refs: The Saechsische Arbeiterzeitung, Dresden, under her brief editorship

stops.name: Leipzig, Sozialreform oder Revolution?
stops.date_confidence: The articles ran in the Leipziger Volkszeitung and were collected as Sozialreform oder Revolution?; sources give 1899 for the articles and 1900 for the book chapter cited here. Month not recorded.
stops.campa: Eduard Bernstein has told the party in print what much of it privately believes, that capitalism is stabilizing, that the collapse is not coming, and that socialism will arrive as the sum of reforms. She answers him in the Leipzig paper, article by article, and then between covers. Her case is not that reforms are worthless but that they are a means of struggle and not an installment plan for a new society, and that a movement which drops the final aim has dropped everything. She knows, and says in the text, that the party she is addressing is already travelling in Bernstein's direction.
stops.quote: Just as all roads lead to Rome so too do we logically arrive at the conclusion that the revisionist proposal to slight the final aim of the socialist movement is really a recommendation to renounce the socialist movement itself.
stops.quote_source: Reform or Revolution (1900), ch. 8, 'Conquest of Political Power'
suggested_refs: Sozialreform oder Revolution?, collected from the Leipziger Volkszeitung articles

stops.name: Zwickau, six weeks for insulting the Kaiser
stops.date_confidence: Sentenced to three months in July 1904 for lese-majeste, entered the Zwickau jail at the end of August, released 15 October 1904 under an amnesty after about six weeks. The exact day of entry is not recorded; 31 August is used to place the stop. The commonly repeated 'three months imprisoned' conflates the sentence with the time served.
stops.campa: She has said in public that the Emperor speaks of the welfare of German workers without knowing anything about how German workers live. The court gives her three months for it. She serves about six weeks in Zwickau before an amnesty lets her out on the fifteenth of October; the day she went in is not recorded anywhere reached here. It is her first prison and the shortest, and she finds she can work inside one. The three months of the sentence and the six weeks actually served are still routinely confused for each other.
suggested_refs: The Zwickau jail, first of her German imprisonments

stops.name: Warsaw, back over the frontier on false papers
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: The Russian Empire has been in revolution since January: Petersburg, the general strikes, the Lodz rising, soviets. She has been writing about it from Berlin for a year and cannot bear to keep doing so. On the twenty-eighth of December she and Jogiches cross into Russian Poland under false names, sixteen years after she was smuggled out, into a city under martial law where the party she founded is being hunted. She goes to edit its paper and to argue in person that the moment is not over.
suggested_refs: The SDKPiL press in Warsaw during the 1905-06 revolution

stops.name: Warsaw, the Town Hall jail and Pawiak
stops.date_confidence: Arrest with Jogiches on 4 March 1906 attested; she passed through the Town Hall jail and Pawiak before the Citadel. Coordinate corrected to the documented position of Pawiak prison on the former ul. Pawia.
stops.campa: The police take them both on the fourth of March. She goes through the Town Hall jail and then to Pawiak, the prison the empire keeps for political cases in Warsaw, and she is held under a false name that the authorities have not yet penetrated. Her comrades outside spend those weeks in a calculation of some delicacy: whether making her identity public brings German and international pressure to bear, or simply tells the Tsarist courts exactly whom they are holding.
suggested_refs: Pawiak prison, Warsaw, political wing

stops.name: Warsaw Citadel, Pavilion X
stops.date_confidence: Release on bail on 28 June 1906, on health grounds, per pl.wikipedia and the Rosa-Luxemburg-Stiftung chronology; en.wikipedia gives 28 July 1906 and names bail of 3,000 roubles paid by her brother Jozef. The two dates are a real and unresolved conflict in the record and are not adjudicated here. Pavilion X has no separate published coordinate; the pin is the Citadel perimeter.
stops.campa: Her last Warsaw prison is Pavilion X of the Citadel, the fortress the Tsar built over the city after 1831 and the place where the leaders of the first Proletariat were hanged the year before she joined the second. She is ill by now. Family money, German party pressure and an international press campaign get her out on bail; her brother Jozef pays three thousand roubles. The date the gate opens is given as the twenty-eighth of June by one chronology and the twenty-eighth of July by another, and no one has reconciled them.
suggested_refs: Pavilion X of the Warsaw Citadel, political prison of the Russian administration

stops.name: Kuokkala, the mass strike written out
stops.date_confidence: The Finnish stay is dated to 1906; the month is approximate and August is used to order the segment. Kuokkala lay in the Grand Duchy of Finland, that is, inside the Russian Empire, which is precisely why it worked as a refuge: Finnish jurisdiction, Russian police at arm's length. Coordinate corrected to the village, today Repino.
stops.campa: Out on bail and forbidden nothing in particular, she goes north to a village of dachas on the Gulf of Finland where the Russian revolutionaries are wintering, Lenin among them, an hour by train from Petersburg. Kuokkala lies inside the Russian Empire and under Finnish jurisdiction, which is exactly what makes it usable. There she writes against the men who run the German trade unions: the mass strike is not a device a committee decides to use, it is what a class does, and organization comes out of the struggle as much as it precedes it. The pamphlet is printed in Hamburg the same year.
stops.quote: Not above, amongst the heads of the leading directing organisations and in their federative alliance, but below, amongst the organised proletarian masses, lies the guarantee of the real unity of the labour movement.
stops.quote_source: The Mass Strike, the Political Party, and the Trade Unions (1906), ch. 8, trans. Patrick Lavin
suggested_refs: Massenstreik, Partei und Gewerkschaften (Hamburg, 1906)

stops.name: Mannheim, the congress that will not have it
stops.date_confidence: SPD congress, September 1906; the day is not fixed here. The Rosengarten is the conventional venue for SPD congresses of the period but was not confirmed for this session; the attested matter is the political outcome.
stops.campa: She brings the mass strike to the party congress and the party congress hands it to the unions. The trade-union leadership has a treasury, contracts, sickness funds and a membership that would lose all of it in a general strike, and it will not have the weapon so much as discussed. She stays in the SPD for another eight years after Mannheim and is never again at its center. The resolution that passes binds the party not to call a mass strike without the agreement of the unions, which is the same as not calling one.
suggested_refs: Protokoll of the SPD Mannheim party congress, 1906

stops.name: Berlin, the party school
stops.date_confidence: She taught political economy and economic history at the SPD Parteischule from 1907 until 1914; the school's street address was not confirmed and this coordinate is an admitted central Berlin placeholder. The October date orders the segment.
stops.campa: The party puts her in front of its own cadres to teach political economy and economic history, and she does it for seven years: functionaries, editors, future deputies, men who will vote the war credits in 1914 and men who will be shot in 1919, all of them taught value and surplus value by her. She thinks she is good at it and says so. Out of the lectures grows a textbook she never finishes, the Einfuehrung in die Nationaloekonomie, assembled from the papers she left and printed after her death. Which street the school stood in has not been established here.
suggested_refs: Einfuehrung in die Nationaloekonomie, assembled posthumously from the Parteischule lectures

stops.name: Stuttgart, the war amendment
stops.date_confidence: The Stuttgart congress of the Second International, August 1907; the stop is placed on the opening of the congress week.
stops.campa: At the Stuttgart congress of the International she sits down with Lenin and with Martov to draft an amendment about the war that everyone in the hall can see coming. The text commits the socialist parties not merely to oppose the war but, should it break out anyway, to use the crisis it creates to hasten the fall of the order that produced it. The amendment passes. It is printed in the proceedings and quoted for seven years, and in August 1914 the parties that voted for it vote the war credits instead.
suggested_refs: The Luxemburg-Lenin-Martov amendment to the Stuttgart antiwar resolution, 1907

stops.name: Berlin-Schoeneberg, Cranachstrasse 58
stops.date_confidence: The address is attested by the commemorative plaque and by de.wikipedia; the years of occupancy are not documented and the date is used only to order the segment. The district is Schoeneberg, not Friedenau, and the coordinate is corrected accordingly. The herbarium is dated 1913-1918.
stops.campa: There is a flat in the Malerviertel with books, a cat, a piano she likes to hear played and a desk under a window. She is a botanist who did not become one. Between 1913 and 1918 she presses plants into albums and writes the name, the place and the date beside each one in a clear hand, and she keeps it up through three prisons. The albums are in the archive now, filed with the political papers, the specimens labelled in the same hand as the pamphlets and the letters out of Wronke.
suggested_refs: Her herbarium of pressed plants, 1913-1918, in the Nachlass Rosa Luxemburg, Bundesarchiv

stops.name: Berlin, Die Akkumulation des Kapitals
stops.date_confidence: Publication year 1913 attested; no month given in the sources used. Coordinate is an admitted central Berlin placeholder rather than a documented address of composition.
stops.campa: She sets out to finish an argument Marx left open in the second volume of Capital, how expanded reproduction is possible at all, and comes out somewhere he did not go: capitalism cannot realize its surplus inside itself, and so must keep breaking into territory that is not yet capitalist. Which makes the gunboat, the concession, the punitive column and the loan to a peasant empire not a moral failure of the system but its metabolism. It is the book her name in the twentieth century rests on. The orthodox economists of her own party attack it as soon as it appears, and she answers them at length in a reply written later, in prison.
suggested_refs: Die Akkumulation des Kapitals (Berlin, 1913), and the Antikritik written in prison in reply to its critics

stops.name: Frankfurt-Bockenheim, do not shoot your brothers
stops.date_confidence: September 1913; the day is not recorded in the sources used.
stops.campa: The state prosecutes her for incitement to disobedience after a meeting in a hall in Bockenheim. She has printed the same argument for a decade; saying it out loud to a working-class audience of military age is what makes it chargeable. The charge opens the last free stretch of her life, and she spends the interval committing the offense again in other towns. What she said was that if the order is given to raise weapons against their French and other foreign brothers, they must refuse it.
suggested_refs: The Bockenheim speech of September 1913, basis of the incitement charge

stops.name: Frankfurt, the courtroom used as a platform
stops.date_confidence: Trial and sentence of one year, February 1914; the day is not fixed here. The second prosecution, over her charge that soldiers were routinely mistreated in the German army, was adjourned rather than heard.
stops.campa: Paul Levi defends her, and she conducts the trial as a public meeting that she happens to be standing trial in, addressing the gallery and the reporters rather than the bench. The sentence is one year. She does not go to prison on it; she appeals, and stays out. When the state opens a second case, over her assertion that recruits are systematically abused in the barracks, she offers to call hundreds of soldiers as witnesses, and that prosecution is quietly adjourned rather than allowed to become a trial of the German army.
suggested_refs: The Frankfurt Landgericht proceedings of February 1914, with Paul Levi for the defense

stops.name: Berlin, the fourth of August
stops.date_confidence: The Reichstag vote on war credits, 4 August 1914, is attested; the Gruppe Internationale forms in the weeks following. Coordinate is a central Berlin placeholder.
stops.campa: The Reichstag delegation votes the war credits under party discipline, unanimously, and the International that met at Stuttgart in 1907 ceases to exist as anything but a set of national parties at war with each other. She is at home when the news comes. Sixteen years of work inside the SPD end in an afternoon. With Karl Liebknecht, Franz Mehring, Clara Zetkin and Jogiches she forms the Gruppe Internationale, which for the first months is a handful of people, a mailing list, and a circular they cannot legally post.
suggested_refs: The Gruppe Internationale, later the Spartakusbund, formed in the weeks after 4 August 1914

stops.name: Berlin, the women's prison on the Barnimstrasse
stops.date_confidence: Imprisonment from 18 February 1915 to February 1916, per de.wikipedia. The Junius text was written here in 1915 and published in June 1916; the two dates are often conflated into a single 1916, which is wrong. Coordinate corrected to the Barnimstrasse in Friedrichshain.
stops.campa: The 1914 sentence catches up with her in February and she begins it in the women's prison on the Barnimstrasse, where she will sit for a year almost to the day. Inside she writes the pamphlet signed Junius, after the anonymous pamphleteer of eighteenth-century London, a hundred pages arraigning her own party for what it did in August 1914. It puts a phrase into the century's mouth that is still quoted by people who have read nothing else of hers. The manuscript goes out of the prison by hand and is printed in June 1916, sixteen months after she wrote it.
stops.quote: Bourgeois society stands at the crossroads, either transition to socialism or regression into barbarism.
stops.quote_source: The Junius Pamphlet (1915, published 1916 under the pseudonym 'Junius'), ch. 1
suggested_refs: Die Krise der Sozialdemokratie, the Junius Pamphlet, written 1915, published June 1916

stops.name: Wronke, the fortress and the birds
stops.date_confidence: Taken into Sicherungsverwahrung, protective custody without ordinary criminal trial, from July 1916; held first in Berlin, then Wronke, then Breslau. The Berlin facility for the first weeks is not identified in the sources. Coordinate corrected to the Wronki prison.
stops.campa: Four months out of the Barnimstrasse she is taken again, this time without trial: protective custody, held at the state's pleasure for as long as the war lasts. After some weeks in Berlin she is moved to the fortress at Wronke in the Posen country. She has a small garden there for a while. Her letters record the wasps, the titmice, the sequence in which things come into flower, and, in the same paragraphs, insomnia, illness and a depression she names without any softening.
suggested_refs: The Wronke prison letters, 1916-1917

stops.name: Breslau, the buffalo in the yard
stops.date_confidence: The letter to Sophie Liebknecht is dated only to the middle of December 1917; the first of the month is used to place the stop.
stops.campa: In the Breslau prison yard soldiers drive a team of buffalo brought as war booty from Romania, overloaded with sacks, and beat one of them with the butt end of a whip until it bleeds. She watches from the window and writes it to Sophie Liebknecht, whose husband is also in prison. She sets down the beast's face, and then her own condition, in the same paragraph, without arranging any distance between the two. Of everything she wrote, the letter about the animal is the most read.
stops.quote: The one that was bleeding had an expression on its black face and in its soft black eyes like that of a weeping child.
stops.quote_source: Letter to Sophie Liebknecht, Breslau prison, mid-December 1917, trans. Eden and Cedar Paul
suggested_refs: Briefe aus dem Gefaengnis, the letters to Sophie Liebknecht, published 1920
sources: marxists.org, 'Letters from Prison to Sophie Liebknecht'

stops.name: Breslau, the manuscript on the Russian Revolution
stops.date_confidence: Written in prison in 1918; month not recorded and the date orders the segment. The original manuscript is considered lost, and the text is known through the edition Paul Levi published in 1922, three years after her death, which is itself a contested act of editorial judgement.
stops.campa: News of what the Bolsheviks are doing reaches her in a cell, incomplete and months late, and she writes an unfinished manuscript that defends the October seizure of power and then refuses to spare its authors. Lenin and Trotsky have dissolved the Constituent Assembly, narrowed the suffrage, and made terror an instrument of administration; a dictatorship in the name of a class, she writes, is not the same thing as the dictatorship of a class. The original of the manuscript is lost. The text exists at all because Paul Levi printed it in 1922, three years after her death, in an edition argued over ever since.
stops.quote: Freedom only for the supporters of the government, only for the members of one party – however numerous they may be – is no freedom at all. Freedom is always and exclusively freedom for the one who thinks differently.
stops.quote_source: The Russian Revolution (1918), ch. 6, 'The Problem of Dictatorship'
suggested_refs: Die russische Revolution, edited from the surviving papers and published by Paul Levi in 1922

stops.name: Breslau, the gate opens
stops.date_confidence: Released 9 November 1918, per both en.wikipedia and de.wikipedia. Some biographies carry 8 November; the two cited encyclopaedias agree on the ninth and the earlier date is not followed here.
stops.campa: The sailors mutiny at Kiel, the garrisons go over one after another, the workers' and soldiers' councils form city by city, and on the ninth of November the Emperor's government ends and a republic is declared twice in one afternoon in Berlin by two different men from two different balconies. In Breslau the prison simply opens. She has been in custody, with a single four-month interval, since February 1915. She is forty-seven years old, ill, grey, and she gets on a train.
suggested_refs: The November Revolution of 1918 and the opening of the political prisons

stops.name: Berlin, arrival and Die Rote Fahne
stops.date_confidence: Reached Berlin on 10 November 1918 per de.wikipedia, the day after release. The office address of Die Rote Fahne was not confirmed and this coordinate is a central Berlin placeholder.
stops.campa: She reaches Berlin on the tenth of November and is at work on a newspaper within days. Die Rote Fahne is edited by two people lately out of prison, herself and Karl Liebknecht. She has ten weeks left to live and spends them writing daily, at a speed that shows on the page. The paper comes out into a city that has soldiers' councils in the barracks, a provisional government of Social Democrats in the chancellery, and machine guns available to anybody with the nerve to go and requisition them.
suggested_refs: Die Rote Fahne, November 1918 to January 1919, under Luxemburg and Liebknecht

stops.name: Berlin, the founding congress of the KPD
stops.date_confidence: The congress ran 30 December 1918 to 1 January 1919; her programme speech was delivered on 31 December. The venue was not independently confirmed and the coordinate is a central Berlin placeholder.
stops.campa: The Spartacists constitute themselves as a party over three days at the turn of the year, and she gives the programme speech on the thirty-first. Then she and Paul Levi argue that the new party should stand candidates in the National Assembly elections, and they lose the vote: the delegates, younger and angrier than she is, choose a boycott. It is on the record, against nearly everything later said about her by admirers and enemies alike, that she was the one urging the ballot. The speech ends on a motto she takes from Faust.
stops.quote: In the beginning was the act.
stops.quote_source: 'Our Program and the Political Situation', speech to the KPD founding congress, 31 December 1918
suggested_refs: Stenographic record of the KPD founding congress, 30 December 1918 to 1 January 1919
sources: marxists.org, 'Our Program and the Political Situation'

stops.name: Berlin, Order Prevails in Berlin
stops.date_confidence: Published in Die Rote Fahne on 14 January 1919, the day before her murder.
stops.campa: The government dismisses Emil Eichhorn from the Berlin police presidency, the crowds come out, the buildings are occupied, and the rising is put down inside a week by Freikorps troops the Social Democratic government has called in against workers. She had argued the rising was premature. When it came she stood with it, and when it was crushed she wrote its obituary the same night, refusing both the government's word for what had happened and her own side's comfort. The article ends: I was, I am, I shall be.
stops.quote: "Order prevails in Berlin!" You foolish lackeys! Your "order" is built on sand.
stops.quote_source: 'Order Reigns in Berlin', Die Rote Fahne, 14 January 1919
suggested_refs: 'Ordnung herrscht in Berlin', Die Rote Fahne, 14 January 1919, her last published article

stops.name: Berlin-Wilmersdorf, Mannheimer Strasse 43
stops.date_confidence: Arrested at Mannheimer Strasse 43, today number 27, at about 20:30 on 15 January 1919, per de.wikipedia. Coordinate corrected to the geocoded address, where a memorial now stands.
stops.campa: She and Liebknecht have been moving from flat to flat for a week, hidden by comrades, refusing to leave the city while the arrests go on. On the evening of the fifteenth a citizens' militia comes to the last of the flats, a friend's apartment in Wilmersdorf, at about half past eight. She is allowed to pack a small bag and she puts a book in it. They are driven across to the Hotel Eden, which the Guard Cavalry Rifle Division has taken over as its headquarters, and which is still a hotel, with a bar, a lobby, and officers drinking in it.
suggested_refs: The memorial at Mannheimer Strasse 27, Berlin-Wilmersdorf, site of the arrest
sources: Wikipedia (de), 'Ermordung von Rosa Luxemburg und Karl Liebknecht'

stops.name: Berlin, the Hotel Eden
stops.date_confidence: She arrived at the hotel around 22:00 and was struck at the main entrance with a rifle butt by the soldier Otto Runge. The killings were carried out on the order of the division's staff officer, Captain Waldemar Pabst, as the Deutsche Biographie entry on Pabst states.
stops.campa: Captain Waldemar Pabst has the division's headquarters in the hotel and a decision to make about two prisoners the government has not asked him to hold. Liebknecht is walked out first, driven into the Tiergarten and shot. She is brought down about two hours before midnight, and at the main entrance a soldier named Otto Runge strikes her twice on the head with his rifle butt and she is carried unconscious to the waiting car. In the lobby, officers watch this and go on drinking.
suggested_refs: Deutsche Biographie, entry on Waldemar Pabst, on whose order the killings were carried out
sources: Wikipedia (de), 'Ermordung von Rosa Luxemburg und Karl Liebknecht'

stops.name: Berlin, the Landwehr Canal
stops.date_confidence: The car had travelled about forty metres when she was shot. The identity of the shooter is a genuine historiographical dispute and is not resolved here: Klaus Gietinger's forensic-historical reconstruction identifies the naval officer Hermann Souchon, while the early official proceedings centred on the transport officer Kurt Vogel, and no contemporaneous conviction established it. De.wikipedia places the disposal of the body in the canal between the Lichtenstein and Cornelius bridges, so 'at or near the Lichtensteinbruecke' is the accurate form.
stops.campa: The car goes some forty metres from the hotel door before someone shoots her in the head. Then the body is driven the short distance to the Landwehr Canal, weighted, and put over the parapet into the water between two bridges in the Tiergarten, where it stays for four and a half months. Nobody is convicted of it. A soldier is punished for the rifle butt, an officer for disposing of a corpse; the man who gave the order dies in his bed in 1970, and had said long before then that he had done what was necessary.
suggested_refs: Klaus Gietinger, Eine Leiche im Landwehrkanal, the forensic-historical reconstruction naming Souchon
Herbert Marcuse's own account of dating his break with the SPD to the killings of 15 January 1919
sources: Wikipedia (de), 'Ermordung von Rosa Luxemburg und Karl Liebknecht'

segments.name: The Canal, the Grave, and the Sentence

stops.name: Berlin, the water gives her back
stops.date_confidence: A female body was recovered from the Landwehr Canal on 31 May 1919, per de.wikipedia's article on the murders, and identified by Mathilde Jacob. Some accounts give 1 June. Identification proceeded by clothing, personal effects and physical characteristics, not by any method a modern forensic service would call conclusive.
stops.campa: On the thirty-first of May a body comes up out of the canal. Mathilde Jacob, who had been her secretary and had carried her manuscripts out of three prisons, identifies it by the clothes and by what is left; no method a modern forensic service would call conclusive is used. Leo Jogiches had spent February publishing in Die Rote Fahne what he had established about the killings, and was still working on them when he was arrested. On the tenth of March a criminal officer named Ernst Tamschick shot him in the back of the head in the Moabit remand prison.
suggested_refs: Jogiches's investigation of the January killings, published in Die Rote Fahne, 12 February 1919
sources: Wikipedia (de), 'Ermordung von Rosa Luxemburg und Karl Liebknecht'

stops.name: Berlin, buried at Friedrichsfelde
stops.date_confidence: Burial 13 June 1919 at the Zentralfriedhof Friedrichsfelde, attested. Coordinate corrected to the Gedenkstaette der Sozialisten; the two lenses of the research disagreed by several hundred metres and this is the surveyed position. In 2009 a Charite pathologist proposed that an unidentified cadaver held at the hospital might be her remains; DNA never settled it, and some reference works now describe the Friedrichsfelde grave as a cenotaph.
stops.campa: She is buried on the thirteenth of June before a procession that fills the road out to Lichtenberg, in a cemetery that will become the burial ground of the German left and then of the East German state. In 2009 a pathologist at the Charite argued that a headless cadaver in the hospital's collection matched her better than the identified body did, and no DNA test settled the matter either way; some reference works now hedge the grave with the word cenotaph. Whether what went into the ground at Friedrichsfelde in June 1919 is her body is a question nobody has closed.
suggested_refs: Reuters and Guardian coverage, May 2009, of Michael Tsokos's Charite hypothesis, an unconfirmed forensic claim
sources: Reuters and The Guardian, May 2009 (not re-fetched during research; reported as unresolved)

stops.name: Friedrichsfelde, the brick monument
stops.date_confidence: Built in spring 1926 to Ludwig Mies van der Rohe's design and unveiled 13 June 1926, the seventh anniversary of the burial; damaged by the National Socialists in February 1933 and dismantled to the foundations in early 1935. The English-language description giving dimensions of twelve metres by six is not corroborated on the German page, and 'January 1935' is not supported.
stops.campa: Seven years to the day after the burial, a wall of clinker brick is unveiled over the graves, designed by Ludwig Mies van der Rohe: blunt projecting blocks laid up out of true, no columns, no allegory, no figure of a mourning woman, a steel star and the letters KPD. It is a monument to the November Revolution built out of the same material Berlin builds its factories and its tenement courtyards from. The regime that comes in 1933 damages it in February of that year and has it taken down to the foundations by the beginning of 1935.
suggested_refs: The Revolutionsdenkmal at Friedrichsfelde, Mies van der Rohe, 1926, destroyed 1935

stops.name: Berlin-Mitte, the square takes her name
stops.date_confidence: Renamed Luxemburgplatz in 1947 and Rosa-Luxemburg-Platz in 1969; the day of the 1969 renaming is not given in the source used and the date is placed at the head of the year.
stops.campa: Bulowplatz held the Communist Party headquarters from 1926, and on the twenty-fifth of January 1933 it held one of the last great anti-Nazi demonstrations in Berlin. Five days later the government changed hands, and the Nazis renamed the square Horst-Wessel-Platz after a dead stormtrooper. Each renaming after that is an argument about whose city this is. Liebknechtplatz in 1945, Luxemburgplatz in 1947, and in 1969 the East German state gives it her name in full: four names in thirty-six years, on the same paving.
suggested_refs: Rosa-Luxemburg-Platz, Berlin-Mitte, formerly Bulowplatz and Horst-Wessel-Platz

stops.name: Friedrichsfelde, her sentence on a banner
stops.date_confidence: The official Liebknecht-Luxemburg march fell on Sunday 17 January 1988, per de.wikipedia's article on Stephan Krawczyk; the germanhistorydocs.org document dated 18 January 1988 is the date of the report, not of the event, and this discrepancy is flagged rather than resolved. The GHDI page confirms the banner and a group of twenty to thirty encircled by some fifty Stasi officers; de.wikipedia puts total arrests that day at 105.
stops.campa: The East German state marches to her grave every January. In 1988 a group in the peace and human rights movement joins the official column carrying a banner with a line of hers on it, the one from the lost Breslau manuscript about freedom for the one who thinks differently. The state is quoting her on its own placards at the same march, in the other direction. The Stasi has the banner down in moments; the report counts twenty to thirty people encircled by some fifty officers, and puts the arrests across the whole day at a hundred and five.
suggested_refs: germanhistorydocs.org, report on the dissident protest at the Liebknecht-Luxemburg memorial march, January 1988
sources: germanhistorydocs.org, 'Protest by Dissidents at the Memorial March for Rosa Luxemburg and Karl Liebknecht'
